objectives.text: Define and distinguish a data structure, an algorithm, a graph and graph traversal, using an example of each.
Identify and explain vertices and edges in a graph and distinguish between directed and undirected graphs.
objectives.criterion: At least 80% of the labels and classifications correct.

objectives.text: Map a real-world problem, such as a network of connected locations, to an appropriate graph representation, naming its vertices, edges and direction.
objectives.criterion: At least 3 of 4 situations modelled correctly.

objectives.text: Explain the purpose of BFS and identify situations in which graph traversal is useful.
objectives.criterion: At least 3 of 4 choices and reasons correct.

objectives.text: Trace BFS manually on a given graph, correctly identifying the next vertex to process, the queue contents, the visited vertices and the traversal order.
objectives.criterion: Correct queue, visited set and next vertex at every step, with at most one error.

objectives.text: Implement BFS in Python using the selected graph representation and a queue, producing the expected traversal for a given input.
objectives.criterion: The ordered and completed code matches the reference solution, including the expected traversal order.

objectives.text: Test and debug a BFS implementation using suitable test cases, including a disconnected graph or a graph containing a cycle.
objectives.criterion: Both faulty versions corrected to match the solution. For each bug, a chosen test case fails the faulty version and passes the correct one.

objectives.text: Use BFS to find the shortest route, measured in number of edges, between two vertices in an unweighted graph, and explain why BFS guarantees it.
objectives.criterion: At least 3 of 4 items correct: finding the fewest edges and the route BFS records, and explaining why BFS guarantees it.
